The hardest conversation in this job is not the one where you tell somebody they have lost. It is the one where somebody has decided to fight and you can see what it is going to cost them. And the mistake every young lawyer makes, including me, is to try to talk them out of it. It never works. It makes the client dig in, and worse than that, it changes what the conversation is about: now it is about you and them rather than about the case. Your job is not to change the decision. Your job is to be certain that the person deciding has the real numbers in front of them. I have also banned a phrase in my own team, and people think I am joking until I explain it. If I were you. The client is not you. He does not have your money, he does not have your two years, and he is not going to be the one sitting in that room. The sentence answers a question nobody asked. Here is the thing I would want somebody to tell me at the start of a career. Clients almost never remember the advice. What they remember, for years, is whether they were told the downside before they decided or only afterwards.

I was told at the beginning that it would take about a year, and that my prospects were good but not certain, and both of those things were honest. The year was two years. I do not hold the estimate against anybody; nobody knows, and the person who told me said so. What I did not expect was what it would take up. I stopped talking about anything else. With everybody. My sister told me eighteen months in that she could not remember the last conversation we had had that was not about the case, and she was right, and I had not noticed. If I were doing it again, the one thing I would change is that: I would keep one part of my life where the case did not exist, deliberately, even if it meant putting the file away on a Sunday. Would I go through with it again? Yes. But with one condition attached, and I say this to everybody who asks me. It was never about the money. If you are going through with something like this for the money, settle. The people who last two years are the ones who need the finding itself, and they know which one they are before they start.

The research on regret has one finding that surprises almost everybody, and it has held up now for several decades. In the short term, people regret the things they did: the thing they said, the money they spent, the decision they rushed. Over a longer horizon, five years, ten years, that flips, and what people report regretting is what they did not do. The second kind is more persistent, and it is much harder to argue with, because the version of your life in which you did the thing is unavailable for inspection. There is a related finding about delay. Putting a decision off feels like keeping your options open, and it is usually the option being chosen. Most decisions that are postponed for long enough end up being made by the calendar rather than by the person. We asked a researcher who studies this what she actually tells people who come to her weighing something up. She said she asks them for one sentence. Write down what the downside is, exactly, in one sentence. Most people, she said, are frightened of something they have never made themselves name, and naming it almost always makes it smaller than it was.
